items.abstract:
<jats:p>The nominee shareholding agreement, as a flexible investment arrangement, caters to the specific needs of the Chinese commercial environment, such as safeguarding privacy, circumventing investment restrictions, and facilitating the intergenerational transfer of family businesses. While such agreements have played a positive role in broadening investment channels and promoting the development of a market-oriented economy, their inherent secrecy and lack of regulatory clarity have also introduced instability and legal uncertainty into the market.
Despite the widespread use of nominee shareholding agreements in China, there is still no comprehensive and explicit legal framework to define their nature or to regulate their use. At the same time, intense academic debate over the legal implications of such agreements continues unabated. Against this backdrop, this research conducts an in-depth examination of the legal issues arising from nominee shareholding agreements, aiming to contribute to the resolution and clarification of the related legal controversies through doctrinal analysis and empirical study.
This research begins by outlining the research background and methodology, followed by an exploration of the application of the concept of the nominee in China, which leads naturally to a broader discussion of nominee shareholding agreements. It first elaborates on the general requirements for contract formation in China, then analyzes the scope and limitations of contractual freedom under the Chinese legal framework. The discussion proceeds to examine the parties involved in nominee shareholding agreements, their characteristics, classifications, academic interpretations, and the applicable legal rules. Furthermore, the research assesses how the principle of contractual freedom influences the formation of nominee shareholding agreements and evaluates their advantages and disadvantages. Finally, by analyzing case studies in conjunction with relevant legal doctrines and drawing on international experience, the research offers recommendations and perspectives for improving the regulation of nominee shareholding agreements under Chinese law.</jats:p>
title: Legal ambiguities of anonymous shareholder under a  nominee shareholding agreement in China

items.abstract: <jats:p>As China’s Company Law approached its sixth revision, clarifying the legal nature and validity of nominee shareholding arrangements was important to achieving a dynamic balance between encouraging investment and safeguarding transactional security. Because trust law recognizes both the independence of trust property and the rigor of fiduciary obligations, nominee shareholding should, unless the beneficial shareholder and nominee shareholder have expressly agreed otherwise, generally be interpreted and organized through the legal framework of a trust relationship. Consistent with the modern rule-of-law principle that private actors may do whatever the law does not prohibit, the validity of nominee shareholding arrangements should be fully respected and effectively protected. The legal effect of nominee shareholding has both an internal and an external dimension. Internally, the law should promote the spirit of contract and a culture of trust and should firmly protect the beneficial shareholder’s rights to information, economic benefits, adjustment of the strategy for exercising shareholder rights, avoidance of unauthorized dispositions of the shares, removal of the nominee shareholder, participation in corporate governance, and conversion into a registered shareholder. Externally, the principle of reliance on legal appearance is the basic rule for resolving conflicts between an undisclosed beneficial shareholder and a bona fide third party. The doctrine of bona fide acquisition should apply, by analogy and with necessary adaptations, to nominee-held shares, thereby safeguarding transactional security and improving share liquidity. In enforcement proceedings, the beneficial shareholder should likewise yield, as a general rule, to bona fide creditors of the nominee shareholder. The appearance principle should not apply, however, where the creditor knew or should have known of the nominee arrangement. To respect party autonomy, the validity of nominee shareholding should follow the orientation of “valid as a rule, invalid only by exception.” The scope of invalid nominee shareholding agreements should be strictly limited. A three-step method should be used to identify mandatory rules whose violation affects validity, and courts should exercise particular caution before invoking public order and good morals as a basis for invalidity.</jats:p>
title: The Legal Nature and Validity of Nominee Shareholding Arrangements

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Nominee shareholding serves legitimate and distinctive functions in corporate practice, but identifying the
<br>
underlying ownership relationship becomes difficult when an undisclosed shareholder and a nominee
<br>
shareholder never executed a written nominee shareholding agreement, or when such an agreement has been
<br>
lost, destroyed, or taken. This article argues that a judicial interpretation of the Company Law should supply
<br>
specific adjudicatory rules for such cases. Courts should adopt an integrative approach to evidence, objectively,
<br>
comprehensively, fairly, and rationally evaluating the evidentiary chain assembled by the alleged undisclosed
<br>
shareholder. They should not atomize that chain into unrelated items and then reject the claim on the ground that
<br>
no single item independently proves the disputed facts. Three categories of evidence are especially important:
<br>
evidence of mutual assent to a nominee shareholding arrangement; evidence that the alleged undisclosed
<br>
shareholder actually exercised shareholder rights; and evidence that the alleged undisclosed shareholder
<br>
subscribed for and paid registered capital or capital reserves. Because founding shareholders of a limited liability
<br>
company stand in a quasi-partnership relationship, their testimony may carry substantial probative value in
<br>
identifying an undisclosed founding shareholder. The personalist character of a limited liability company may
<br>
also give meaningful weight to the testimony of later shareholders. Courts should exercise discretion prudently
<br>
and with an inclusive and rational judicial mindset. More broadly, evidence of shareholder status should be
<br>
differentiated among source evidence, presumptive evidence, and opposability evidence. The internal
<br>
identification of an undisclosed shareholder must rest primarily on source evidence, whereas opposability
<br>
evidence is principally relevant to external legal relations involving third parties.</jats:p>
title: Identifying Undisclosed Shareholders in the Absence of a Written Nominee Shareholding Agreement

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper examines the impact of controlling shareholders’ stock pledge on institutional shareholding using the sample of Chinese listed firms. Stock pledge means shareholders use stock of listed firms as the pledged assets to apply for loans. Using the sample of Chinese listed firms during the period of 2005 to 2015, this paper documents controlling shareholders’ stock pledge decreases institutional shareholding significantly and such relation is more remarkable in the subsample of firms facing more tunneling activities conducted by controlling shareholders. Additionally, using the method of test on mediating effect, this paper finds that controlling shareholders’ stock pledges reduce institutional shareholding through decreasing cash dividends. Collectively, these findings document that institutional investors are sophisticated investors for they always take account for risks owing to controlling shareholders’ stock pledges when selecting stock.</jats:p>
